summary: Defines ways to sign and encrypt XMPP content from end to end, so that only the sender and receiver, rather than the servers in between, can read or vouch for a message.

eli5.summary: Instead of handing your note to a mail carrier unsealed, you lock it in a box only your friend can open and sign it so they know it is from you.

questions: how does xmpp end to end encryption work
what is the xmpp e2e element
what algorithms must xmpp e2e support
how does xmpp prevent replay of signed messages
subtitle: How XMPP clients can sign and encrypt messages and presence end to end using S/MIME wrapped in an e2e element.

tldr.problem: XMPP servers sit between users and can read or alter stanzas in transit, and instant messaging requirements call for integrity, replay protection and confidentiality between the two endpoints.
tldr.mechanism: The sender builds a Message/CPIM, PIDF or application/xmpp+xml object, signs and/or encrypts it with S/MIME and CMS, and places the result in a CDATA section inside an e2e element of the stanza.
tldr.outcome: Only directed messages, directed presence and other stanzas sent to a specific user are covered, and the method also works through an XMPP-CPIM gateway.

facts.label: Required encryption
facts.value: RSA key transport, AES-128 in CBC mode

today: RFC 3923 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is referenced by RFC 3922 for secured traffic through an XMPP-CPIM gateway.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 3923 defines end-to-end signing and object encryption for XMPP. A sender can sign and/or encrypt an instant message sent to a specific recipient, sign and/or encrypt presence directed to a specific user, and sign and/or encrypt any arbitrary XMPP stanza directed to a specific user. This helps XMPP meet the requirements in RFC 2779.

The idea is that only the two endpoints, rather than the servers between them, can read the content or vouch for who sent it.
sections.eli5: You write to a friend through helpers who pass the note along. This lets you seal and sign the note so the helpers cannot read or change it.

sections.title: Requirements and Scope
sections.content:
The method MUST meet the minimal IM and presence security requirements of RFC 2779. These include confidence that a message has not been corrupted or tampered with, has not been recorded and replayed, and is readable only by entities the sender allows. Clients MUST be able to use these means but MUST NOT be required to use them at all times.

It MUST also interoperate with non-XMPP systems that support CPIM. Before signing or encrypting, a message must conform to the CPIM Message Format and presence to PIDF. Signing MUST use S/MIME signatures with CMS SignedData, and encryption MUST use S/MIME encryption with CMS EnvelopedData.

Out of scope are discovery of support for the protocol, signing or encrypting groupchat messages, broadcast presence (only directed presence is covered), and applications other than instant messaging and presence.
sections.eli5: The rules say the lock must stop tampering, copying and snooping. They also say people can choose not to use it, and that it should work with other chat systems too.

sections.title: Securing Messages and Presence
sections.content:
To secure a message, the sending agent MUST generate a Message/CPIM object, sign and/or encrypt both its headers and content, and place the result in an XML CDATA section inside an <e2e/> child of the <message/> stanza. The <e2e/> element is qualified by the urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-e2e namespace.

Signing produces a multipart/signed object with two parts: the Message/CPIM object and an application/pkcs7-signature part. Encryption produces an opaque encrypted blob.

Presence works the same way, using an application/pidf+xml object inside a <presence/> stanza. That stanza MUST carry a to attribute, so it must be directed presence.
sections.eli5: You write the note, then sign it or lock it in a box. The box goes inside a special envelope called e2e that rides inside the normal chat message.

sections.title: Securing Arbitrary XMPP Data
sections.content:
Messages and presence cover only the lowest common denominator. XMPP also has the <iq/> stanza and extension elements. Because the CPIM message format can encapsulate any MIME type, the RFC defines an XML media type, application/xmpp+xml, to hold arbitrary XMPP data.

Its root element is <xmpp/>, which MUST contain exactly one child, a message, presence or iq stanza when the default namespace is jabber:client or jabber:server. The encoding MUST be UTF-8. Such an object is signed and/or encrypted and then wrapped in an <e2e/> CDATA section like the others.
sections.eli5: For things that do not fit the normal note, there is a bigger carrying case that can hold any chat packet, which then gets sealed the same way.

sections.title: S/MIME Rules
sections.content:
Certificate enrollment is outside the scope. A receiving agent MUST provide some way to retrieve certificates, and user agents SHOULD be able to request a recipient's certificate in a signed reply. Certificates SHOULD carry the sender's address as both an im: URI and a pres: URI in two separate subjectAltName entries, and the JID in the stanza's from MUST match one of them (ignoring the resource). Receivers MUST check this match.

The transfer encoding MUST be binary. If a stanza is both signed and encrypted, it SHOULD be signed first, then encrypted. Senders SHOULD include their certificate with at least one encrypted message every five minutes during an active session, and SHOULD NOT include it more than once every five minutes. Senders SHOULD attach a signature to each encrypted stanza.

Timestamps help prevent replay. They MUST be UTC, and a receiver MUST verify that the timestamp is within five minutes of the current time. It SHOULD verify the timestamp is greater than any timestamp received in the last 10 minutes that passed the check. Failures are shown as "old timestamp", "future timestamp" or "decreasing timestamp".

Mandatory algorithms are SHA-1 and RSA (PKCS #1 v1.5) with SHA-1 for signing, plus RSA (PKCS #1 v1.5) key transport and AES-128 in CBC mode for encryption.
sections.eli5: Your ID card must match the name on the note. Notes carry the time, and a note that is too old or from the future looks suspicious, like a replayed message.

sections.title: Recipient Error Handling
sections.content:
The RFC lists five cases for a receiver. If it does not understand the protocol, it MUST do exactly one of: ignore the <e2e/> extension, ignore the whole stanza, or return <service-unavailable/>. On success, it MUST NOT return an error.

If timestamps fail the checks, the receiver MAY return <not-acceptable/> with an optional <bad-timestamp/>. If the signature cannot be verified, it SHOULD return <not-acceptable/> with an optional <unverified-signature/>. If it cannot decrypt, it SHOULD return <bad-request/> with an optional <decryption-failed/>. Stanzas with invalid signatures or that cannot be decrypted SHOULD NOT be shown to the recipient.
sections.eli5: If a sealed note arrives and you cannot open it or its signature looks fake, you tell the sender and do not show it as if it were fine.

sections.title: Secure Communication Through a Gateway
sections.content:
A gateway between XMPP and a non-XMPP service can carry secured traffic. For traffic from XMPP to the non-XMPP side, it MUST strip the XMPP wrapper (everything through the <e2e> and </e2e> tags) to reveal the multipart S/MIME object and route that onward. For the opposite direction, it removes the other service's wrapper and adds the XMPP one.

The wrapped S/MIME object MUST be immutable and MUST NOT be modified by the gateway. This is why RFC 3922 ignores most extension content but passes through content in the e2e namespace.
sections.eli5: The translator in the middle may only move the sealed box from one carrier to another. It must never open it or change what is inside.

sections.title: Namespace and Media Type Registration
sections.content:
The namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-e2e is registered for signed and encrypted XMPP content. It has no inherent semantics. The meaning of the wrapped object comes from the specification for Message/CPIM, application/pidf+xml or XMPP core, and versioning is the job of those protocols.

The RFC also registers the MIME media type application/xmpp+xml, with UTF-8 as the required charset and intended usage COMMON. An appendix gives a descriptive, non-normative schema for the e2e element and the three error condition elements.

The security section says the whole memo concerns security, and it refers to the security considerations of RFC 2779, XMPP core and the XML media types.
sections.eli5: The RFC puts its new envelope name and its new packet type into the official list so nobody else uses them by accident.
